title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
abstract: Foundational model of choice under risk: people evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, weight losses more heavily than equivalent gains (loss aversion), and distort probabilities. Explains risk-seeking in the domain of losses.
pattern_explained: Why retail traders ride losers and avoid realizing losses; underpins the disposition effect.

title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
abstract: Catalogs the heuristics (representativeness, availability, anchoring-and-adjustment) people use under uncertainty and the systematic biases they produce.
pattern_explained: Anchoring on recent prices and availability of WSB narratives drives retail mispricing.

title: Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice
abstract: Introduces mental accounting: people segregate money into non-fungible mental buckets and evaluate gains/losses per account, leading to framing-dependent decisions.
pattern_explained: Framing of a position (house money vs cost basis) shapes hold/sell decisions independent of fundamentals.

title: The Disposition to Sell Winners Too Early and Ride Losers Too Long
abstract: Names and models the disposition effect: investors realize gains too quickly and hold losers too long, driven by loss aversion and mental accounting.
pattern_explained: Predicts retail behaviour when a hyped ticker turns: holding into drawdowns rather than cutting.

title: Does the Stock Market Overreact?
abstract: Finds prior extreme losers outperform prior extreme winners over subsequent years — evidence of systematic overreaction and long-horizon mean reversion.
pattern_explained: When retail euphoria peaks and prices overshoot, subsequent mean reversion is the base-rate expectation.

title: Noise
abstract: Argues markets are populated by noise traders who trade on noise as if it were information, providing liquidity but pushing prices away from value.
pattern_explained: Frames retail crowds as noise traders whose activity can decouple price from fundamentals.

title: Noise Trader Risk in Financial Markets
abstract: Shows that unpredictable noise-trader sentiment is itself a risk that deters arbitrage, so mispricings can persist and even be profitable for noise traders.
pattern_explained: Explains why institutional 'smart money' may not immediately correct a retail-driven mispricing.

title: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency
abstract: Documents medium-term momentum: past 3-12 month winners continue to outperform past losers, a robust anomaly inconsistent with weak-form efficiency.
pattern_explained: Momentum can sustain a rally even as insiders sell — short-horizon continuation before reversal.

title: Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?
abstract: Using brokerage records, shows individual investors sell winners at a markedly higher rate than losers, confirming the disposition effect empirically.
pattern_explained: Empirical retail evidence for the hold-losers behaviour Prism flags after a hype unwind.

title: Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors
abstract: The most active individual investors underperform the market net of costs; overtrading, not bad stock selection alone, erodes returns.
pattern_explained: Core retail-underperformance evidence; the lens for high-churn WSB names.

title: Boys Will Be Boys: Gender, Overconfidence, and Common Stock Investment
abstract: Overconfident investors trade more and earn lower returns; the effect is stronger among men, linking overconfidence to excessive trading.
pattern_explained: Overconfidence as the mechanism behind euphoric, high-volume retail participation.

title: All That Glitters: The Effect of Attention and News on the Buying Behavior of Individual and Institutional Investors
abstract: Individual investors are net buyers of attention-grabbing stocks (high volume, news, extreme returns); institutions are far less attention-driven.
pattern_explained: Directly explains WSB mention spikes: retail buys attention, institutions don't — a divergence engine.

title: Insiders' Profits, Costs of Trading, and Market Efficiency
abstract: Insiders earn abnormal profits and their aggregate trading predicts market and cross-sectional returns; insider buying is more informative than selling.
pattern_explained: Establishes that insider transactions carry predictive content — the basis for the insider advocate.

title: Are Insider Trades Informative?
abstract: Aggregated insider activity predicts future returns, concentrated in small firms; insider buying is informative while routine selling is largely not.
pattern_explained: Insider buying > selling as a signal; cautions that much insider selling is uninformative (e.g. diversification).

title: Decoding Inside Information
abstract: Separates 'routine' insiders (predictable, calendar-driven trades) from 'opportunistic' ones; only opportunistic trades predict returns and news.
pattern_explained: Justifies Prism distinguishing programmatic 10b5-1 / routine sales from discretionary, informative insider sales.

title: Who Gambles in the Stock Market?
abstract: Identifies retail investors' preference for lottery-type stocks (low price, high volatility, high skewness), especially among certain demographics.
pattern_explained: Why retail crowds into speculative, high-volatility names — the profile of many WSB favourites.

title: Maxing Out: Stocks as Lotteries and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
abstract: Stocks with extreme recent daily returns (high MAX) earn low subsequent returns, consistent with demand for lottery-like payoffs.
pattern_explained: Lottery-stock demand overprices high-MAX names — a headwind after a retail-driven spike.

title: Investor Sentiment and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
abstract: Constructs an investor-sentiment index and shows that when sentiment is high, speculative, hard-to-value stocks subsequently underperform.
pattern_explained: High retail sentiment predicts underperformance for speculative names — quantifies the euphoria signal.
